title: The probability arcade
objectives: Explain how temperature reshapes a toy probability distribution.
Distinguish sampling settings from factual verification.
prediction: A snack raffle favors tea over juice and water. If we make the odds more even, is water now guaranteed to win?
explanation: A text model produces scores for possible next tokens. Sampling converts scores into probabilities and picks from those probabilities. The top choice can be common without being the only possible choice.

Temperature is one way to reshape probabilities. In this toy, divide each score by a positive temperature, apply exp, and normalize so probabilities add to one. Lower temperature makes the highest score dominate more; higher temperature flattens the distribution.
exp is a mathematical function that turns these scores into positive values. You do not need to memorize its formula today. Inspect how the final probabilities change when the temperature changes.

Temperature is not a truth knob. A lower value can repeat a false claim more consistently. A higher value does not guarantee creativity. Actual models may recommend specific defaults or restrict which settings are supported. We will check the configured model before offering a live control.
analogy_limit: The raffle helps explain sampling probabilities. Our fixed snack scores are invented, and the code displays probabilities rather than sampling. It is not a factuality experiment or a guarantee about a particular hosted model.

python_example.expected_output:
T = 0.5
tea: 0.87, juice: 0.12, water: 0.02
T = 2.0
tea: 0.51, juice: 0.31, water: 0.19
walkthrough: The toy scores are inputs, not observed truth ratings.
Subtracting the maximum score helps numerical stability without changing the normalized probabilities.
The dictionary comprehension builds one weight per snack; division by total normalizes them.
Two-decimal display rounding can make the printed values add to 1.01. The unrounded values sum to approximately one.
Temperature zero is excluded here to avoid division by zero; this toy does not implement greedy decoding.

game.title: Snack Raffle
game.instructions: Predict what the two displayed distributions imply. Remember that likelihood and correctness are different. Get two of three right.

rounds.prompt: At T=0.5, tea has about 87% probability. What does that mean for sampling?

choices.text: Tea must be the healthiest drink
Water is impossible
Tea is likely, but not guaranteed in one draw

feedback.a: Sampling can still select a lower-probability option.
feedback.b: The probabilities do not measure health or truth.
feedback.c: Water still has positive probability in this toy.

rounds.prompt: What happened when the toy temperature rose from 0.5 to 2.0?

choices.text: The most likely snack became certain
The training data grew
The probabilities became more even

feedback.a: The highest probability decreased, rather than becoming certain.
feedback.b: The distribution flattened, increasing relative chances for lower-score options.
feedback.c: Only the sampling transform changed; no data was added.

rounds.prompt: Your chatbot repeats a wrong date. Should lowering temperature count as verification?

choices.text: Yes, consistent dates are always true
No, the claim still needs evidence
Yes, because probabilities become sharper

feedback.b: Sharper probability is not factual support.
feedback.c: Use source evidence and evaluations to check the date.

questions.prompt: Why divide each weight by the total weight?

choices.text: To normalize the probabilities
To change the words into source citations
To retrain the model

feedback.a: Normalized probabilities sum to approximately one before display rounding.
feedback.b: Normalization has nothing to do with citations.
feedback.c: This transform changes sampling probabilities, not learned scores.

questions.prompt: Does the example code actually draw a random snack?

choices.text: No, it only computes and prints probabilities
Yes, print randomly chooses a dictionary key
Yes, exp picks one

feedback.a: exp produces weights; a separate sampling step would choose an option.
feedback.b: No random selection function is called.
feedback.c: print only displays the constructed text.

questions.prompt: What should we verify before adding a live temperature slider?

choices.text: The configured model's supported settings and recommendations
That all models have identical controls
That higher values guarantee truth

feedback.b: Generation controls can differ across models.
feedback.c: Build the live control around actual provider support.

build.title: Test a flatter distribution
build.instructions: Add T=1.0 to the example. Before running it, predict whether tea's probability will lie between the T=0.5 and T=2.0 values. Check the unrounded sum of probabilities.
criteria: Tea's probability at T=1.0 is approximately 0.665 and lies between the two earlier values.
The unrounded probabilities sum to approximately one; you do not mistake display rounding for extra probability.
hints: Use abs(sum(odds.values()) - 1) < 1e-9 to check the sum with a small numerical tolerance.
build.reference_solution:
With the example function defined:
odds = probabilities(1.0)
print(round(odds['tea'], 3))  # 0.665
print(abs(sum(odds.values()) - 1) < 1e-9)  # True

reflection: How would you explain to someone why a consistent chatbot answer can still be wrong?
tutor_context: Explain invented logits, normalized probabilities, and positive temperature with a raffle analogy. Do not equate temperature with accuracy or creativity. Explain rounding and avoid deep calculus.

visual.title: Turn scores into a probability menu
visual.inputs: Tea has score 2, juice 1, and water 0. Compare temperatures 0.5 and 2.
visual.operation: Subtract the largest score, exponentiate scaled scores, and divide by their total.
visual.output: Lower temperature concentrates the distribution; higher temperature spreads it out.
visual.limit: The scores are authored. This toy prints probabilities and never samples a word. Temperature does not verify facts.

frames.title: Start with scores
frames.explain: Scores are not probabilities: they do not add to one. Tea is highest in this authored menu.

frames.title: Scale the differences
frames.explain: At T=0.5, subtracting peak=2 gives scaled differences 0, -2, -4. exp turns these into positive weights.

frames.title: Normalize a cooler menu
frames.explain: Divide each weight by their sum. Tea has about 86.68% probability. Two-decimal display rounding can make printed values sum to 1.01.

frames.title: Warm it up
frames.explain: At T=2.0 the gaps shrink. Tea stays most likely, but juice and water receive more probability.
frames.console:
T = 0.5
tea: 0.87, juice: 0.12, water: 0.02
T = 2.0
tea: 0.51, juice: 0.31, water: 0.19

challenge.question: What changes when temperature rises in this example?

choices.text: Water must become the most likely word
choices.feedback: Scaling these score gaps does not reverse their order. Compare the two bar shapes.

choices.text: The distribution gets flatter; tea still ranks first
choices.feedback: Exactly. More spread does not mean the ranking reverses.
